title: And can it be (Charles Wesley, 1738)
hookLine: my chains fell off, my heart was free
tomorrow: a hymn once titled 'Faith's Review and Expectation.' know it?
last: MY SOUL, MY LIFE, MY ALL.

lines: THE LAST BELL. THE CAST OFF.
cards: The last bell of the last exam. The cast cut off after six weeks. The day the debt is paid.
Freedom has a feeling, and people describe it with their bodies: I could breathe, I felt light. So what does freedom feel like from the inside?
Charles Wesley, John's brother, wrote a hymn that answers with a prison cell, and one line that ends in three short words: my chains fell off.

teach.b: "Long my imprisoned spirit lay Fast bound in sin and nature's night; Thine eye diffused a quickening ray, I woke, the dungeon flamed with light; My chains fell off, my heart was free; I rose, went forth, and followed thee."

Wesley is borrowing a scene from Acts. Peter sits chained in prison, an angel comes, "a light shined in the prison," and then: "his chains fell off from his hands." Wesley takes Peter's story and says me.
My chains. My heart. That's the Christian answer: freedom from sin, through Christ, told as if you were in the cell.
Now a neighbor who tells freedom the same way.

teach.h: PASSOVER: AS IF YOU CAME OUT.
teach.b: At Passover, Jewish families retell the Exodus, the people of Israel brought out of slavery in Egypt.
And the Mishnah teaches, in a paraphrase, that in every generation a person should see themselves as if they personally came out of Egypt. Not they. Me.
That much is shared: an old rescue, told in the first person, so it happens again in the one telling it. And the honest difference.
Passover remembers a whole people's freedom from real slavery, retold each year around a family table.
Wesley's hymn sings one soul freed from sin by Christ's death, usually in church.
Two ways of saying me, each in its own words.

how: Methodists and other Christians sing And can it be, often standing; at Passover, Jewish families retell the Exodus at the seder table, each generation telling it as their own.

games.q: what does “and can it be” mean?
o: a Christmas carol asking how a baby could be a king
a question Peter asked the angel who opened his cell
Charles Wesley's hymn of wonder at being set free

games.q: chains and freedom — tap the pairs.
p: his chains fell off from his hands
as if you came out of Egypt

s: 'my chains fell off' comes from nowhere in the Bible
it borrows Peter's prison in Acts 12: a light shined, and his chains fell off from his hands.
the Mishnah teaches that each generation should see itself as if it came out of Egypt
Passover tells the Exodus in the first person, the way the hymn says my chains.
Passover and the hymn celebrate the same freedom
they share the first person. Passover remembers a people freed from slavery; the hymn, one soul freed from sin through Christ.

games.q: at a friend's seder, her little cousin says, 'we were slaves in Egypt.' your brother whispers, 'but that was ages ago.' what's the best answer?
o: it's told in the first person on purpose, so the rescue is theirs too.
she's mixed up; it's only a history lesson about other people.
it means her own family were literally slaves recently.
games.why: the Mishnah teaches each generation to see itself as if it came out of Egypt. Wesley's hymn does something like it with Peter's chains: me, my, I.

practice: Name, silently, one chain that has fallen off in your life: a fear, a habit, a grudge, a long sickness. Then stand up and walk slowly across the room and back, the way the hymn ends: I rose, went forth.
Sit down again and let your hands rest open.

wordCard.voice: And can it be. Charles Wesley's hymn of wonder, where Peter's prison becomes my prison, and the chains fall off me.

orig.note: Greek: chains. the word in Acts 12:7 when Peter's chains fell off his hands.

carryVoice: Your line: my chains fell off. An old rescue, sung as if it happened to the singer. Talk tomorrow.
